passage:
Wednesday.

Recess was brilliant today. Our group has this running joke about Mr Menon's 'seven-minute stories' that go on for twenty. Farhan does the voice, Aman does the hand gestures, and by the end I was crying with laughter. Naveen joined us last week and stood at the edge not laughing. I think he hasn't got the reference. I felt bad, so I explained it to him. Then someone made a joke about Naveen's accent, and everybody laughed except him. I laughed a second too long and then stopped. His face went closed.

I'm going to tell the boys tomorrow that accent jokes aren't funny, and I'll say sorry to Naveen. 😕

qa.q: What is the group's running joke about?
qa.a: It is about Mr Menon's 'seven-minute stories' that go on for twenty.

qa.q: What was Naveen probably feeling when everyone laughed at the accent joke?
qa.a: He probably felt excluded and hurt, since his face went closed and he didn't laugh. He was also already standing at the edge.

qa.q: What would you advise Farhan to do about the accent jokes?
qa.a: Tell the group calmly that jokes about someone's accent are unkind, and apologise to Naveen for laughing.

qa.q: How might the other boys see the accent joke?
qa.a: They may think it was harmless fun, without noticing how it landed on someone new.

grounding: Banter builds belonging but can exclude, and jokes about someone's accent can harm.

passage:
In the small town of Narsinghpur, Chaitanya's group had a joke for everything. Somebody only had to say "the mango incident" and the whole bench would collapse laughing, remembering Sonu falling off the school wall in Class 6.
Yamini had joined in July. On Tuesday someone said "mango incident" again, and the boys doubled over. Yamini smiled politely, then looked down at her tiffin and ate in silence.
Chaitanya noticed. It happened most days. She laughed a second late, or not at all.
At the tap after lunch he said, "You must think we're mad. Want the mango story? It's worth it."
Yamini laughed. "I thought it was something rude."
He told her, with actions. She laughed properly this time.
Next day, Yamini said something about the geography teacher's umbrella, and Chaitanya's group had a new joke. She was in on it from the start.

qa.q: When had Yamini joined?
qa.a: Yamini had joined in July.

qa.q: What did Yamini's polite smile and silent eating suggest?
qa.a: It suggested she felt left out and a bit awkward, unable to share the joke because she didn't know the story.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya turn the banter into something that included Yamini?
qa.a: He noticed her silence and offered to tell her the mango story at the tap, which let her into the shared reference.

qa.q: How might Sonu feel about the mango incident being a group joke?
qa.a: Sonu seems to share the laughter since it's an old, friendly memory, but it would be worth checking he still finds it funny.

grounding: The scene shows in-group banter building belonging while excluding a newcomer, and a friend including her.

passage:
In a flat in Manchester, Esther's friends were piled on the sofa watching a baking show. Nadia had moved from Lagos two years ago.
When a contestant said "water," Tom did an exaggerated impression of Nadia's accent. Everyone laughed. Nadia laughed too, a beat late, then pulled her knees up to her chin.
Two minutes later he did it again, louder. "Say 'butter,' Nadia!"
Esther watched Nadia's smile. It was fixed, like a photograph. Esther's own ears felt hot.
"Tom, stop," she said lightly. "We have a thousand jokes. We don't need that one."
There was an awkward pause. Tom shrugged. "It's just banter."
"Not if only one person's being joked about," Esther said. Then, to break the silence, "Remember when you set the toaster on fire?"
Everyone laughed, including Nadia, properly this time. Later she texted Esther: "Thanks for earlier."

qa.q: How long ago had Nadia moved from Lagos?
qa.a: Nadia had moved from Lagos two years ago.

qa.q: What did Nadia's late laugh and fixed smile suggest?
qa.a: They suggested Nadia felt hurt and embarrassed by the accent jokes, laughing along only to fit in.

qa.q: What did Esther do that helped?
qa.a: She calmly asked Tom to stop, explained why it wasn't really banter, and switched to a shared joke that didn't target anyone.

qa.q: How does Tom see the accent impressions?
qa.a: Tom sees them as "just banter," not noticing that they single out Nadia and rely on her difference.

grounding: The scene shows banter that builds belonging turning harmful when it relies on mocking someone's accent, and a friend stopping it.

passage:
The hostel common room was loud after dinner. Bhupen was in form. He'd already done his impression of the mess cook and of the warden's slippers, and everyone was howling.
Then Gautam walked in. Gautam had failed Class 11 and was repeating the year with them.
"Oh look, Senior Gautam!" Bhupen called out. "Here to guide us juniors? Second time lucky, bhai!"
A big laugh. Gautam smiled, sat down at the carrom board, and didn't speak for the rest of the evening. He left early.
Bhupen felt something off. The joke had got a bigger laugh than the slippers. So why did it feel bad?
Next morning at the tap he said, "Gautam, the senior thing. That was about something that actually hurts. I won't do it again."
Gautam nodded slowly. "Thanks. Do the slippers one again, though. That's actually funny."

qa.q: What had Gautam failed?
qa.a: Gautam had failed Class 11.

qa.q: What did Gautam's silence and leaving early suggest?
qa.a: It suggested he felt hurt and humiliated by a joke about failing, even though he smiled.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who, like Bhupen, feels something off after a joke?
qa.a: Check whether the joke touched someone's real pain, and if so, apologise plainly and drop it, as Bhupen did.

qa.q: How might the others who laughed see the "Senior Gautam" joke?
qa.a: They probably saw it as part of Bhupen's usual banter, without thinking about how it felt to be the one repeating a year.

grounding: The hostel scene shows banter building belonging but a joke about someone's pain causing harm, and the joker repairing it.

Dear Rehana,
The group chat misses you, and so do I. We still call ourselves the Back Bench Pakoras and still reply to everything with "as per the prophecy", which makes no sense to anyone but us, and that's the whole point. I wanted to tell you something, because you'd have had an opinion. On Monday a new girl, Meenal, sat with us at lunch and we did the full pakora routine. She kept laughing half a second late, looking from face to face. Then Anu did the voice, the one copying Mr Das's stammer, and everyone cracked up, and I laughed too. Meenal didn't. She went quiet and left early. Later I found out her brother stammers. I felt sick. On Tuesday I explained the prophecy joke to her from the start, and told Anu the voice has to go. Anu sulked for a day. Meenal is in the chat now.
Miss your terrible puns,
Sudha

qa.q: What did the group call themselves?
qa.a: They called themselves the Back Bench Pakoras.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling after learning about Meenal's brother?
qa.a: Sudha felt sick with guilt and shame for laughing at the stammer voice; there may also have been worry about how Meenal now saw the whole group.

qa.q: Which choices on Tuesday helped, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the prophecy joke let Meenal into the in-group, and telling Anu the voice has to go stopped a joke built on someone's pain.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Meenal on Monday?
qa.a: Meenal laughed half a second late, looking from face to face, so the private jokes left her outside; the stammer voice then hurt, and she left early.

grounding: It shows banter and shared references building belonging but shutting out a newcomer, and a joke mocking a stammer hurting even when framed as fun.
